case_name: Pradip Sonavane & Anr. v. DSSD Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
holding_summary: The complainants took possession of their redeveloped flat in the 'Shri Nandadeep Bhavan' project in 2016 but filed their consumer complaint against the developer and housing society only in 2026, alleging deficiency of service discovered later. A bench of Justice A.P. Sahi (President) and Bharatkumar Pandya dismissed the complaint as barred by limitation under Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, holding that the cause of action arose on the date possession was taken and does not become a continuing wrong merely because defects were discovered years afterward.
why_it_matters: Homebuyers who delay filing a consumer complaint over redevelopment or construction defects risk having it dismissed outright on limitation grounds — the clock runs from possession, not from when the deficiency is noticed.

case_name: Raintree Boulevard Apartment Owners Association v. L&T Realty Developers Ltd.
holding_summary: The Association, representing owners in the Raintree Boulevard development at Byatarayanapura, Bengaluru, sought revocation of the registration of L&T Realty's Elara Celestia project and demolition of commercial buildings, alleging modifications were made without the two-thirds allottee consent required under Section 14(2)(ii) of RERA. K-RERA, comprising Chairman Rakesh Singh and Member G.R. Reddy, dismissed the complaint, holding that the two-thirds consent requirement is triggered only where a proposed alteration goes beyond what the registered agreement for sale itself already permitted or the allottees had pre-consented to.
why_it_matters: Developers can rely on modification rights already built into the registered agreement for sale without separately re-securing two-thirds allottee consent each time, so long as the change stays within what allottees contractually agreed to upfront.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. v. Sh. Jamuna Dass
holding_summary: A former Tax Assistant in the Income Tax Department, who superannuated on 31 December 2011 and was convicted by a Special Judge on 23 January 2012, argued his gratuity claim should not remain frozen while his criminal appeal against that conviction stayed pending before the High Court. A Division Bench of Justices C. Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar held that Rule 69(1)(c) of the CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972 operates as a statutory bar — not merely an enabling provision — and gratuity cannot be paid so long as either departmental or judicial proceedings remain pending, with the claim reviving only once the appeal concludes.
why_it_matters: Government employers can continue withholding gratuity through the entire pendency of a criminal appeal, not just through the original disciplinary or trial stage, giving employees facing pending appeals a longer wait before any gratuity claim revives.

case_name: Agriculture Produce Market Committee, Deesa v. National Horticulture Board & Ors.
holding_summary: The APMC at Deesa had received a Capital Investment Subsidy from the National Horticulture Board, routed through NABARD, for construction/expansion/modernisation of cold storage facilities for horticultural produce; NABARD later decided to withdraw the subsidy and recover the amount already disbursed, a decision the NHB upheld. A Single Judge had set aside the withdrawal and held the APMC entitled to the full subsidy; the Supreme Court bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih examined the scheme's conditions in resolving whether that withdrawal and recovery decision was justified.
why_it_matters: Agricultural market bodies and cooperatives receiving central capital-investment subsidies for storage infrastructure should maintain clear documentation of scheme-compliance, since courts will scrutinise the funding agency's own withdrawal conditions closely before disturbing a recovery decision.

case_name: Bank of Baroda v. IDBI Bank Ltd. & Ors. (In the matter of Reliance Communications Infrastructure Ltd.)
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: After the resolution plan for Reliance Communications Infrastructure Ltd. was approved, the Committee of Creditors, at a meeting held on 27 October 2023, passed a resolution by 67.55% majority to reassign and reallocate proceeds of the 'Reliance Bhutan Loan' in favour of financial creditors who had dissented from the plan; IDBI Bank and SBI objected. The NCLT held the CoC had no power to alter the plan's distribution mechanism once approved, and a two-member NCLAT bench of Justice Ashok Bhushan (Chairperson) and Barun Mitra dismissed Bank of Baroda's appeal, holding that the CoC's commercial wisdom operates only up to the point of plan approval and cannot be used afterward to rework how sale or recovery proceeds are distributed among creditors.
why_it_matters: Financial creditors sitting on a CoC cannot revisit or rework an approved resolution plan's distribution formula after the fact, even by a large majority vote — once approved, the plan's payout mechanism binds assenting and dissenting creditors alike and is not open to post-approval renegotiation.

case_name: ADV Industrial Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: The GST refund authority declined to release a Rs. 19.33 crore ITC refund that an appellate authority had already sanctioned, on the ground that the Department intended to challenge the appellate order. The Telangana High Court held that an appellate order remains operative unless stayed, modified or set aside, that merely proposing or subsequently filing an appeal does not suspend it, and that Section 54(11) of the CGST Act lets a refund be withheld only where the Commissioner forms an opinion — after giving the taxpayer a hearing — that release is likely to adversely affect revenue because of malfeasance or fraud, not merely because the Department disagrees with the appellate order.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers who win a GST refund at the first appellate stage cannot be made to wait indefinitely merely because the Department says it plans to appeal — the refund authority must actually invoke Section 54(11)'s malfeasance/fraud test, with a hearing, or release the money.

case_name: JCB India Ltd. v. Anonymous Persons/Entities & Anr. (arising from dispute with Krishna Auto Riders Pvt. Ltd.)
holding_summary: After JCB India's dealership dispute with Krishna Auto Riders Pvt. Ltd. (KARPL) was referred to arbitration, anonymous online accounts allegedly linked to KARPL began using JCB's name, logos and other brand identifiers, and circulated videos and Instagram reels falsely claiming two JCB India officers had been arrested. Justice Jyoti Singh found JCB had established a prima facie case and that the balance of convenience favoured relief, granted an ex parte ad interim injunction restraining the anonymous parties from using JCB's marks and logos in a manner suggesting affiliation, and directed Google and Meta to take down the offending videos and reels.
why_it_matters: Brand owners facing anonymous online accounts that misuse their trademarks and spread false claims tied to an underlying commercial dispute can secure fast ex parte injunctive relief plus platform-level takedown directions against Google and Meta, without first identifying the individuals behind the accounts.

case_name: PayU Payments Pvt. Ltd. v. Visa Worldwide Pte. Ltd., Yes Bank, ICICI Bank & Ors.
holding_summary: PayU challenged acquiring banks' and Visa's deductions aggregating Rs. 68.82 crore from its settlement amounts as Interchange Reimbursement Fee (IRF), arising from a dispute over merchant category code classification, and questioned the validity of Visa's private IRF compliance mechanism under Section 24 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Justice Subramonium Prasad directed the Reserve Bank of India to nominate a senior payments-sector officer to mediate (not adjudicate) the dispute within 30 days, ordered status quo on past disputed transactions, restrained further deductions from PayU's settlements during mediation, and barred Visa from issuing final IRF determinations on the disputed claims pending the process; the matter was listed for further hearing on 27 October 2026.
why_it_matters: Payment aggregators facing unilateral interchange-fee deductions by card networks and acquiring banks now have a judicial template for freezing further deductions and securing RBI-facilitated mediation before the dispute is finally determined, rather than having to accept the network's own private compliance mechanism as final.

case_name: Haryana Power Purchase Centre v. Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd. (and connected petition)
holding_summary: Siwana Solar Power Projects, operating a 5 MW solar plant in Bhiwani, Haryana under a February 2014 Power Purchase Agreement, obtained a Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission order in May 2026 directing HPPC to pay a higher tariff of Rs. 6.44/kWh; HPPC appealed. A bench of Officiating Chairperson Seema Gupta and Judicial Member Virender Bhat set aside HERC's May 2026 order and held Rs. 5.68/kWh — the rate fixed in the original PPA — to be the binding tariff between the parties, relieving HPPC from paying the higher rate and associated differential amounts with interest.
why_it_matters: Discoms and renewable generators disputing a tariff revision should scrutinise whether a state regulator's enhanced rate is actually supported by the underlying PPA terms — APTEL will enforce the contractually agreed tariff over a regulator's own revised figure where the PPA itself does not justify the increase.

case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: After an arbitrator was appointed under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 through the Delhi International Arbitration Centre, the arbitral proceedings were terminated because the petitioner could not pay the DIAC's fees; the petitioner sought a judicial waiver or deferment of arbitral fees on grounds of financial incapacity, and a direction to frame a support mechanism for indigent claimants. The Delhi High Court dismissed the petitions, holding that Section 38 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act does not contemplate any exception for a party's financial incapacity, that the statutory framework permits suspension or termination of proceedings when the required deposit is unpaid without carving out an indigence exception, and that creating financial-support mechanisms for indigent arbitration parties is a policy matter for the legislature, not the courts.
why_it_matters: A claimant or counter-claimant who cannot afford an arbitral tribunal's fees has no judicial recourse to a fee waiver or deferment under the current law — arbitral proceedings can lawfully terminate for non-payment regardless of the party's financial capacity, until Parliament legislates otherwise.

case_name: [Homebuyer] v. BPTP Ltd. (Park Spacio, Sector 37D, Gurugram)
citation: Haryana Real Estate Regulatory Authority, Gurugram Bench
holding_summary: BPTP had collected Rs. 1,16,545 in maintenance charges from a homebuyer in its Park Spacio project before handing over physical possession, and had withheld possession despite full payment of the sale consideration; the builder-buyer agreement contained no clause authorising advance maintenance collection. The Gurugram bench of the Haryana RERA ordered BPTP to refund the full amount with 11% annual interest from the date of collection, awarded Rs. 1 lakh for mental agony and harassment plus Rs. 50,000 in litigation costs, and held that a promoter cannot make pre-possession maintenance payment a precondition for handing over a unit, characterising BPTP's conduct as an unfair trade practice.
why_it_matters: Homebuyers asked to pay maintenance charges before they receive possession — with no such clause in their builder-buyer agreement — have a clear RERA precedent to recover the amount with interest, plus compensation, rather than treating the payment as a valid precondition to possession.

case_name: Sharan Bihari Agarwal & Ors. v. M.K. Gupta
court: Madhya Pradesh High Court, Jabalpur Bench
holding_summary: A Food Inspector had seized coriander powder from a train pantry car in 2004 on suspicion of adulteration; the accused were prosecuted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 but were never informed of their statutory right under Section 13(2) of the Act to have the counterpart sample independently analysed by the Central Food Laboratory. Justice Vivek Agarwal held that Section 13(2) confers a valuable, substantive right on an accused whose exercise depends on being informed of it, that failure to so inform vitiates the prosecution, and invoked Section 482 CrPC to quash the criminal case and set aside the charges.
why_it_matters: A food adulteration prosecution can be quashed outright if the accused was never told of the statutory right to get the sample independently tested at the Central Food Laboratory — prosecuting authorities must build this notice into their procedure or risk losing the case regardless of the sample's actual contents.

case_name: M/s Singla Traders v. State of Haryana & Ors.
holding_summary: A Food Safety Officer in Kaithal seized plant and machinery worth about Rs. 17.20 lakh from Singla Traders, a milk-products manufacturer, on 14 November 2025; the firm challenged the seizure by writ petition. Justice Jagmohan Bansal held that Food Safety Officers acting under Sections 33-42 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 have no power to seize plant and machinery — such power vests solely in a court, exercisable after conviction, or with a Designated Officer following the Act's precise statutory protocol — and quashed the seizure.
why_it_matters: Food business operators facing seizure of their processing equipment by a Food Safety Officer (rather than through a court or the statutorily prescribed Designated Officer process) have a clear precedent to have the seizure quashed as exceeding the officer's statutory authority.

case_name: P B Agro LLP v. Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: P B Agro LLP, master licensee of the VIMAL brand, filed a writ petition in Delhi after the Assistant Commissioner (Food), FDA Greater Mumbai, issued a show-cause notice under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 to three of its brand ambassadors over an advertising campaign for its Elaichi and Pan Masala products; the petitioner argued Delhi jurisdiction on the basis that it operated from Delhi, paid the ambassadors from Delhi, and that FSSAI and the Central Consumer Protection Authority are headquartered in Delhi. The Delhi High Court dismissed the petition for want of territorial jurisdiction, holding that neither the petitioner's own presence in Delhi nor FSSAI's location there could confer jurisdiction, that mere impleadment of FSSAI without any relief sought against it or action attributable to it does not suffice, and that Maharashtra courts were the appropriate forum under forum conveniens since the impugned notice was issued there.
why_it_matters: A food business cannot manufacture Delhi jurisdiction over a state FDA's show-cause notice merely by suing from its Delhi office or naming FSSAI as a party — the challenge must be filed where the notice was actually issued.

case_name: Tata Capital Financial Services Ltd. v. Neel Motors LLP & Ors.
holding_summary: After Neel Motors LLP went into liquidation, Tata Capital sought to proceed with arbitration against the individual personal guarantors, who argued that pending Section 95 insolvency applications against them triggered an interim moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC. Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan held that Section 96(4), inserted with effect from 26 May 2026 to exclude personal guarantors to corporate debtors from the interim moratorium, applies retroactively to Section 95 applications that were already pending as of that date, since the phrase 'where an application is filed' covers anything filed and still under adjudication on the effective date.
why_it_matters: Lenders holding personal guarantees can resume or continue arbitration and recovery action against guarantors even where a Section 95 insolvency application predating the May 2026 amendment is still pending, closing off a moratorium that guarantors had used to stall recovery.

case_name: Rukhmani Keshwani (Trading as Vishwas Agarbatti Store) v. Raju Agarbatti Works & Anr.
holding_summary: The plaintiff, claiming prior use since 1995 of the 'RADHEY KRISHNA' trademark and trade dress for agarbattis, had her infringement suit returned by a Trial Court for want of territorial jurisdiction since both parties operated from Rajasthan. A Division Bench of Justices C. Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla restored the suit, holding that the Rajasthan-based defendants' IndiaMart listings (complete with GST details) that were accessible and enabled purchase from Delhi amounted to purposeful availment and targeting of the Delhi market, sufficient to confer territorial jurisdiction — mere accessibility of a website is not enough, but purposeful digital targeting is.
why_it_matters: Plaintiffs in IP suits can found territorial jurisdiction in a forum based on a defendant's online marketplace listings and evidence of actual purchases there, even where neither party is physically based in that forum, expanding the reach of e-commerce-era jurisdiction doctrine.

case_name: Spherion Solutions Private Limited v. Additional Commissioner Adjudication CGST Delhi North & Ors.
holding_summary: Ruling on a challenge to a GST DRC-07 summary demand order, a Bench of Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain held that input tax credit blocked under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules remains legally unavailable for debit and so cannot be treated as 'payment' satisfying the mandatory pre-deposit for a GST appeal under Section 107(6) of the CGST Act — blocking merely immobilises credit, whereas Section 107(6) requires actual appropriation. The Court allowed the petitioner to file its statutory appeal within four weeks without rejection on limitation, and clarified the pre-deposit need not come solely from the Electronic Cash Ledger but may be met from any lawfully available, debitable amount in the Electronic Credit Ledger.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers whose ITC has been blocked under Rule 86A cannot use that blocked credit to satisfy the GST appeal pre-deposit and must arrange payment from the cash ledger or other available credit, though genuine appeals will not be time-barred purely because of an ITC block.
